# Sharp source costs for an arbitrary density multiplier

This is a continuous auxiliary theorem. It does not assert an allocation of
the fibers of a mixed-integer body into compatible source groups.

Let d>=1 be an integer, k>=2 a real number (in particular, an integer),
q=1+1/d, and gamma=(d/(d+1))^d. Let B be a d-dimensional convex body,
0<=eta<=1_B dx, alpha=eta(B)/|B|, and let g be the centroid of

    rho=1_B dx+k eta.

The ACTUAL source cost of a closed halfspace H containing g is

    v=(|B intersect H|+eta(H))/|B|.

The coefficient of eta in this cost is ONE, regardless of k. This is the
quantity controlled by a pointwise cap argument for an average of k source
points.

## 1. The sharp fixed-alpha theorem

For every fixed alpha in [0,1], the sharp lower bound on v is the attained
minimum of s+r over

    0<=s<=1,  0<=r<=min(alpha,s),  s+alpha-r<=1,

    q(1+k alpha)s^(q-1)
       >=1+k r^q+k(s+alpha-r)^q-k s^q.                 (1)

Every minimizing pair has 0<s<1 and equality in (1). It is realized by
a simplex with eta equal to volume on two parallel quantile bands.

Proof. Normalize |B|=1, and move H parallel until its boundary contains g.
The centroid is interior to B because rho has density at least one there.
Thus its ordinary cap volume s is strictly between zero and one. Every
hyperplane has zero B and eta measure, so closed boundaries cause no loss.

For the scalar coordinate X in the cap direction, let U(t)=|B cap {X>=t}|.
Brunn--Minkowski makes U^(1/d) concave on the projection interval: the
Minkowski interpolation of two caps is contained in the intermediate cap.
The projection is atomless and has positive section density in its interior,
so U(X) is uniform on [0,1] under volume on B. The pushforward of eta has a
density h in [0,1], with integral alpha and integral over [0,s] equal to r.
Jensen at the rho centroid gives

    (1+k alpha)s^(1/d)
      >=d/(d+1)+k integral_0^1 t^(1/d)h(t)dt.

The increasing integrand has smallest integral, with these two prescribed
masses, when h fills [0,r] and [s,s+alpha-r]. Indeed subtracting the leftmost
interval indicator, and then the integrand's cutoff value, makes the
integrated difference nonnegative. This gives exactly (1).

The feasible domain is compact and nonempty: s=1,r=alpha is feasible and
has strict slack (q-1)+k alpha(q-alpha^(1/d))>0. At s=0 feasibility fails.
If a minimizer has strict slack, decrease s and r together when r>0, or
decrease s alone when r=0. All remaining constraints persist for a small
decrease and the objective falls. Thus equality holds. Since s=1 forces
r=alpha, it is excluded at a minimizer.

For realization, take a volume-one simplex and its vertex barycentric
coordinate X, so U(X)=(1-X)^d. Set eta equal to volume on

    {U(X) in [0,r] union [s,s+alpha-r]}.

Equality in (1) says that the rho centroid has X-coordinate 1-s^(1/d).
Its cap in this direction therefore has B mass s and eta mass r. This
proves exact sharpness, not just a necessary relaxation. In particular
the fixed-alpha optimum is gamma at alpha=0 and 2 gamma at alpha=1.

A one-variable version is also available. For r in [0,alpha], let t(r)>0
be the unique positive root in s of equality in (1), without imposing the
other constraints. Its left-minus-right side is strictly increasing in s:

    derivative >=q(q-1)(1+k r)s^(q-2)>0.              (2)

Here concavity of x^(q-1) bounds the increment over alpha-r by
(q-1)(alpha-r)s^(q-2). The slack tends to a negative value at zero and to
positive infinity at infinity. Therefore minimize

    r+max{r,t(r)}

over precisely those r in [0,alpha] for which
max{r,t(r)}<=1-alpha+r. This is an equivalent attained scalar formulation.

## 2. Optimizing alpha removes the second band exactly

Write Xi_(d,k) for the infimum of the actual source cost over ALL alpha,
all B, all eta, and all containing caps. The slack in (1), at fixed s,r,
has alpha derivative

    k q[s^(q-1)-(s+alpha-r)^(q-1)]<=0.              (3)

Thus reducing alpha to r preserves feasibility and does not change s+r.
Conversely alpha=r is allowed. Consequently

 Xi_(d,k)=min {s+r: 0<=r<=s<=1,
                        q(1+k r)s^(1/d)>=1+k r^q}. (4)

This is the global infimum of the UNNORMALIZED cost relative to |B|.
The conclusion (3) is not claimed for the ratio (s+r)/(1+alpha).

Put u=(r/s)^(1/d) in [0,1] and t=s^(1/d). For each u, the unique equality
root t=t_k(u)>0 is

    q t+k u^d(q-u)t^(d+1)=1.                       (5)

It is less than one. For this u, increasing t increases the cost, so

    Xi_(d,k)=min_(0<=u<=1) (1+u^d)t_k(u)^d.         (6)

All equality configurations in (6) are actual simplex examples with
eta its top vertex cap of volume r=u^d t_k(u)^d. Since r<=s, the entire
eta mass lies inside the tested centroid cap, as required.

## 3. Exact finite-k optimizer

Let u_* be the unique root in (0,1) of

    u_*^d+d u_*-d=0,

and define, for 0<=u<u_*,

    Z(u)=d(1-u)-u^d,
    D(u)=(d+1)(1-u)-u^(d+1),
    K(u)=D(u)^d/Z(u)^(d+1).

Then K is continuous and strictly increasing, with

    K(0)=1/(d gamma),       K(u)->infinity as u->u_*.

If k<=1/(d gamma), the exact minimum in (6) is gamma at u=0.
If k>1/(d gamma), there is a unique u in (0,u_*) with K(u)=k, and

    Xi_(d,k)=(1+u^d)[Z(u)/D(u)]^d,
    s=[Z(u)/D(u)]^d,       alpha=r=u^d s.           (7)

For integer k>=2 the first case occurs only when d=1,k=2, at equality.
For d=1 the formula simplifies to

    Xi_(1,k)=[sqrt(3(k+1))-2]/k,  k>=2.

The independently proved complete fixed-alpha interval formulas appear in
`candidate 04fb8b3cc0275a7f`.

Proof. Implicitly differentiate (5). For 0<u<1 the sign of the derivative
of (1+u^d)t_k(u)^d is the sign of

    1-k t_k(u)^d Z(u).                             (8)

For example the numerator after the positive factors are removed is
q t[1-k t^d Z]; this also proves the formula when d>1, where the derivative
at u=0 itself vanishes. If Z<=0, (8) is positive. If Z>0, evaluate the
left side of (5) at t0=(k Z)^(-1/d). Its value is

    t0 D/Z=(K(u)/k)^(1/d).

Since the left side of (5) increases strictly in t, (8) is negative
when k>K(u), zero when k=K(u), and positive when k<K(u).

For monotonicity of K, direct differentiation gives

 (log K)'=d(d+1)[(1+u^(d-1))/Z-(1+u^d)/D].

The numerator of the bracket, after multiplication by positive ZD, is

 (1+u^(d-1))D-(1+u^d)Z
   =(1-u)[1+u^d+u^(d-1)(d+1-d u)]>0.

Moreover D=q Z+u^d(q-u), so D remains positive at u_*. The claimed
endpoint values and uniqueness follow. Thus the sign changes just once,
from negative to positive, precisely in the second case. Substitution of
(8)=0 in (5) gives t=Z/D and then K(u)=k, proving (7).

For d>=2, the elementary binomial bound (1+1/d)^d<d+1 gives
d gamma>d/(d+1)>1/2, so the threshold is strictly less than two. For d=1
it equals two. This proves the last assertion without an omitted endpoint.

## 4. Sharp asymptotics and explicit finite lower bounds

Put E_*=u_*^d and

    A_d=(q E_*-E_*^q)/(1+E_*)^q,
    C_d=A_d^(-1/q).

Equivalently E_*^(1/d)+E_*/d=1. Then, for each fixed d,

    Xi_(d,k)~C_d k^(-d/(d+1)) as k->infinity.        (9)

In particular C_1=sqrt(3). The examples in (7) explicitly attain Xi at
every finite k and supply the sharp asymptotic extremizers.

Here is a proof with finite inequalities as well. For any feasible (s,r,
alpha), put E=r/s, Q=(s+alpha-r)/s>=1 and v=s+r. Equation (1) gives

 1<=q s^(q-1)+k s^q{q(Q+E-1)-E^q-Q^q+1}.

The expression qQ-Q^q is decreasing for Q>=1, so the braces are at most
qE-E^q. On [0,1] the unique maximum of

    A(E)=(qE-E^q)/(1+E)^q

is at E=E_*: its derivative has the sign of
1-E^(q-1)-(q-1)E. It follows that

    1<=q v^(1/d)+k A_d v^q.                       (10)

Let R_(d,k)>0 be the unique root of equality in (10). Thus EVERY source
cost satisfies v>=R_(d,k). If Rplus is the unique positive root of

    q[v/(1+E_*)]^(1/d)+k A_d v^q=1,

then the actual one-band example E=E_* gives

    R_(d,k)<=Xi_(d,k)<=Rplus_(d,k).                (11)

Multiplying both roots by k^(1/q) and passing to their scalar equations
shows that both tend to C_d; their first terms tend to zero and their
second terms tend to A_d times the qth power. This proves (9) rigorously.

The normalized sharp constant

    XiNorm_(d,k)=inf (|B cap H|+eta(H))/(|B|+eta(B))

has the SAME sharp asymptotic C_d k^(-d/(d+1)). A useful fully explicit
bound, using Section 5 below, is

 XiNorm_(d,k)>=Xi_(d,k)/[1-1/k+Xi_(d,k)/gamma]
              >=R_(d,k)/[1-1/k+R_(d,k)/gamma].     (12)

Indeed Section 5 gives alpha<=v/gamma-1/k. The function
v/(1-1/k+v/gamma) increases strictly for k>1, so (12) follows from
v>=Xi>=R. For the matching asymptotic upper bound, take the exact examples
(7); then r<=s<=Xi tends to zero, so division by 1+alpha=1+r has no effect
on the leading constant. Equations (9) and (12) give the claimed limit.

Thus no coefficient c>0 independent of k can make

    |B cap H|+eta(H)>=c gamma (|B|+eta(B))

valid for this density class. In particular a proposed coefficient tending
to 1/2 as k grows is false, with completely explicit simplex extremizers.

## 5. Comparison with the linear group-budget bound

For every k>=2 and every alpha, the following still holds:

    v>=gamma(1/k+alpha).                            (13)

For completeness the scalar Fenchel proof is included. Set G=1/gamma,
c0=1/(d+1), U=1/s, E=r/s, Q=(s+alpha-r)/s, and

    phi(x)=x-x^q/q.

Dividing (1) by q s^q gives

    phi(U)+k phi(Q)+k phi(E)>=k c0.                (14)

The elementary one-variable maximum is

    phi(x)+a x<=c0(1+a)_+^(d+1),   x>=0.

Use a=1/d on U and Q, and a=-(G-1)/d on E. Since
(1+1/d)^(d+1)=q G, (14) implies

 U+kQ-k(G-1)E
 <=(d/(d+1)){(k+1)q G+k B_d-k},
 B_d=[1-(G-1)/d]_+^(d+1).

This is at most k(G+1), provided

    B_d<=1+q-qG/k.                                (15)

It suffices to prove (15) at k=2. Equivalently

    2d B_d<=4d+2-(d+1)G.

The binomial theorem gives G>=2, and G<e<11/4. An elementary last bound
is e<=8/3+(1/24)/(1-1/5)=87/32<11/4. For d>=3 the right side is greater
than (5d-3)/4>=d, while
B_d<=(1-1/d)^(d+1)<1/2. To see the last inequality, apply the binomial
bound (1+1/(d-1))^(d-1)>=2 and retain the extra square factor. For d=2
the two sides are respectively 27/128 and 13/4; for d=1 they are zero
and two. This proves (15) in every dimension. Finally,

    (1+k alpha)/s=U+kQ+kE-k<=kG(1+E),

which is (13).

There are also alpha-sensitive bounds requiring no Fenchel step. A single
bathtub interval in Section 1 gives

    L=gamma[(1+k alpha^q)/(1+k alpha)]^d,
    v>=max{L,2L+alpha-1}.                           (16)

Thus one may take the maximum of (7)'s Xi, (13), and (16) for any prescribed
alpha. The exact fixed-alpha answer remains Section 1, not this maximum.

If k equal-mass source submeasures of mass a are averaged into eta<=1_B,
with integer average index, and their budgets and the B-volume budget are
disjoint parts of the original measure, a containing ambient cap catches at least one
source point whenever it catches their average. Hence its original mass
is at least |B cap H|+eta(H), while its centroid numerator uses
1_B+k eta. Formula (13) gives gamma(|B|+k a)/k. The new global bounds
give an additional uniform scale C_d k^(-d/(d+1))|B|, but (9) and (12)
show why the two-source improvement relative to |B|+a cannot stay bounded
away from zero for large groups. No partition, reuse of source mass, or
common output-density constraint across several groups is proved here.
